newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing defends McDonnell merger at EU hearing.
newsitem.headline: Boeing defends McDonnell merger at EU hearing.

text.p: Boeing Co executives met EU officials and aviation industry counterparts on Thursday armed with boxes of documents to defend their merger with McDonnell Douglas against charges of unfair competition.

Boeing's presentation marked the first day of a two-day, closed-door hearing organised by the European Commission, the EU's competition watchdog, to allow the U.S. manufacturer and its competitors to air their views about the takeover.

Boeing representatives, including executive vice-president of the commercial airplane group Dick Albrecht and the head of the merger transition team, Jerry King, declined any comment as they emerged for lunch. Others were equally tight-lipped.

The Commission started a full probe into the $14 billion merger in March worried that Boeing, which already controls 60 percent of the world market for commercial jet aircraft, will reinforce its position to an extent that could harm fair competition in the 15-nation European Union.

The hearing, which is being attended by Boeing's only serious rival European consortium Airbus Industrie, is part of the EU's merger control procedure to help the Commission reach its final decision due by July 31.
The two-day meeting is not due to produce any decisions or official statements.
"We are respecting the right of defence and the right for interested parties to put questions," a Commission source said, adding that the probe was proceeding according to schedule.
Boeing had replied to the Commission's objections, detailed in a 40-page dossier on May 21, with a stack of documents about 10 centimetres (four inches) thick, the source said.
Evidence supplied to the hearing by the Seattle-based company appeared even weightier, with Boeing officials arriving laden down by several heavy boxes.

Friday will see the turn of Airbus's managing director Jean Pierson, the consortium's partners and other interested parties to provide evidence on the implications of the merger, Airbus and other sources said.
Pierson said earlier this year that in the long term, the merger would "pose a problem for Europe's civil aviation industry" but thought it was inevitable.

Daimler-Benz Aerospace and British Aerospace BAe, which together with France's Aerospatiale and Construcciones Aeronauticas of Spain control Airbus, have been the most active in opposing Boeing's plans and in pushing for the transformation of Airbus into an independent company.
Lockheed Martin Co was also expected to be represented at the meeting.
Boeing has rejected Commission charges that its deal will damage competition, saying that McDonnell Douglas's market share of new commercial jet sales is only four percent.
But there are many McDonnell Douglas aircraft in European airline fleets for which the Commission believes Boeings will be the "natural" replacements.

According to Association of European Airlines figures, of the passenger jet aircraft flown by AEA members last year, 47 percent were Boeings, 22 percent McDonnell Douglas, 20 percent Airbus and 11 percent other manufacturers.
Figures for aircraft on order looked better for the European consortium, which held 43 percent of the 301 aircraft on order compared with Boeing's 45 percent.
